newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Report shows Lion boxes on with IRD.
newsitem.headline: Report shows Lion boxes on with IRD.

text.p: Tax looks set to remain a contentious issue between Lion Nathan and the inland revenue authorities in New Zealand and Australia for some time, according to the brewer's annual report published on Thursday.
The company incurred a tax charge of $74.2 million in the year to August, compared with a $1.8 million credit the previous year.

In New Zealand "while the Inland Revenue Department's (IRD) assessment has impacted on earnings, all payments have been made on a without prejudice' basis, and Lion Nathan does not acknowledge liability," chief executive Doug Myers said in his
The amounts paid represented the IRD's view on a range of issues.
"The matters are in dispute, and the directors believe an amount will be recovered," he says.

In April, when the increased tax charge was first reported, Lion Nathan executive director Mike Smith declined to say what issues were disputed but said they were not related to the Cook Islands tax commission of inquiry.

The company paid $14.8 million to the IRD in April in relation to the now-completed tax audit of the period 1985 to 1990 which began in 1988. In addition, there was a further $6.5 million charge against earnings against which tax losses had previously been applied.
Meanwhile in Australia, after advice from legal and tax advisors, the group has made no provision for the outcome of a tax audit.

"The group is unable to quantify the extent, if any, of any ultimate taxation liability of this audit, including whether any amended assessment will be issued, penalties determined, or the extent to which the utilisation of prior years' losses will be denied.
"In the event that any adverse assessment should ultimately arise it will be vigorously contested,'' Mr Myers says.
Current tax losses in the group are expected to run out in the 1997 financial year with tax payments, and further imputed dividends beginning the following year.

For 1995-96, Lion Nathan's bottom-line profit fell 26 percent to $150.4 million. The higher tax bill more than cancelled out a 12 percent rise in pre-tax earnings to $224.4 million, from $200.3 million in the previous 12 months .
During the August year, the group paid governments $880.5 million in taxes, including excise, sales tax and other duties, Myers adds.
